name: Film noir still photography
summary: Black-and-white stills with one hard light, deep shadow and a figure caught in a graphic frame. The look comes from the 1940s crime film, and it stays alive in fashion, posters and portraits.

philosophy.core_thesis: Darkness holds the story, so the picture shows only as much light as the mood needs.
design_principles: Use a single hard source, a spot or a bare bulb, at 45° to 90° from the lens axis.
Hold a key-to-fill ratio of 16:1 (4 stops) or more, and let half the face fall into black.
Cast a pattern on a wall: blinds, a lattice or a doorway, with 3 to 7 bars.
Use a 50mm to 85mm lens at f/2.8 to f/5.6 and shoot slightly from below or at a Dutch tilt of 5° to 15°.
Pose the figure with a hat, a cigarette or a gun, in a doorway or on stairs.
Print on a hard grade with true black at 0% and a single highlight at 95–100%.
anti_patterns: Soft, even light with open shadows
Clean modern sets with no texture
Digital noise that looks like a filter
Cartoon props that break the mood

composition.framing: Tight vertical or wide 1.37:1; the frame is cut by shadow and edge.
composition.viewpoint: Slightly below the face, or at a Dutch tilt of 5° to 15°.
composition.geometry: Diagonals of blinds, stairs and doorways; the figure sits in a pool of light.
composition.subject_placement: Off centre, with 40–70% of the frame in shadow.

principles.rule: Hold a key-to-fill ratio of 16:1 or more, with 40–70% of the frame in near-black.
Use 3 layers: a hard key, a rim light at 1 stop under it and a background pattern at 2 stops under.
Cast 3 to 7 bars of shadow that run on a diagonal to the face.
Leave 40–60% of the frame as black space on the side the figure looks away from.
Let 1 lit eye or hand take the highest luminance, at 95–100%, with no second highlight above 80%.

light.quality: Hard and small: a spot with a snoot, a Fresnel or a bare bulb.
light.direction: Side or low front, 45° to 90° from the lens, with cutters and cookies to throw patterns.
light.time_of_day: Studio, or at night with a street lamp

lens_and_camera.format: Medium format or 35mm; digital full frame as a modern equivalent
lens_and_camera.focus: Focus on the lit eye; let the rest fall off.

colour_and_grade.treatment: High-contrast black and white with deep shadows and a single bright accent.
grade_recipe: Convert to monochrome with a red filter mix (R 70, G 30, B 0), to darken skies and deepen lips.
Set the black point at 0% and the white point at 99%.
Apply +45% midtone contrast with a steep S-curve.
Burn the edges by −1 stop and dodge the eye by +0.5 stop.
Add a light haze (clarity −10) in the highlights for a glow around the key.
colour_and_grade.grain: Tri-X 400 pushed to 1600: coarse, with open mid-grey

subjects: a detective or a stranger in a hat
a woman in a long coat
subject_and_staging.staging: Full set: a doorway, a lamp, a blind and a wall; the maker places the cutters first and then the figure.
subject_and_staging.direction: Give the sitter a secret and a direction to look; hold still for 1/60s.

workflow: Develop with a high-contrast developer, or push the film by 2 stops.
Print on grade 4 paper with heavy burning at the edges.
Dodge the eye and the cigarette tip.
Frame in a dark mat to keep the black.
post_processing.output: A deep-black 8×10 in print, or a high-contrast digital file at 4:5 or 1.37:1.

emotion.target_response: Suspense and unease: the viewer feels watched and wants to know what is in the dark.

use_cases: image prompts for moody night scenes
avoid_when: The brief needs warmth, family or clarity of detail in shadows.
The subject must read as friendly.

modifiers.how: Add a large soft fill at 8:1, move to colour and keep one deep shadow side; shoot at f/8 for the garment.
Drop the set and use a real street at night, with a 35mm lens at f/2, ISO 1600 and 1/125s.

sources.title: Paul Schrader, Notes on Film Noir (Film Comment, 1972)
Alain Silver and James Ursini (eds.), Film Noir Reader (Limelight, 1996)
